title: Long Mott (Dow / X-energy): Report on the Safety Aspects of the Long Mott Generating Station Construction Permit Application [['Letter', 'Report, Miscellaneous']]

documents.text:
UNITED STATES
                                    NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION
                               ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON REACTOR SAFEGUARDS
                                       WASHINGTON, DC 20555 - 0001

                                                    October 16, 2026




The Honorable Ho K. Nieh
Chairman
U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
Washington, DC 20555-0001

SUBJECT:       REPORT ON THE SAFETY ASPECTS OF THE LONG MOTT GENERATING
               STATION CONSTRUCTION PERMIT APPLICATION

Dear Chairman Nieh:

During the 739th meeting of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS), held
October 6 through 9, 2026, we completed our review of the safety aspects of the Long Mott
Energy, LLC (LME) construction permit (CP) application for the Long Mott Generating Station
(LMGS), a single utilization facility comprising four small modular high-temperature gas-cooled
Xe-100 reactors and associated common facilities, and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory
Commission (NRC) staff's associated Safety Evaluation Report (SER). Our LMGS Design
Center Subcommittee reviewed this matter on May 5, 2026, September 1, 2, and 15, 2026.
During these meetings, we had the benefit of discussions with the NRC staff and
representatives of LME and X-energy, LLC (X-energy). Our review also benefited from prior
NRC staff and ACRS reviews of topical reports (TRs) and from the referenced documents.

This report fulfills the requirements of Section 182b of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as
amended.1

CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

1. The LMGS CP application describes the principal design criteria, preliminary design, safety
   analyses including a probabilistic risk assessment (PRA), research and development
   program, and other applicant commitments. The NRC staff concludes in their draft SER
   that the CP application is sufficiently complete for the construction-permit stage. Our review
   supports issuance of the construction permit.



1 Section 182b of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA) states, in part, “The Advisory Committee on

Reactor Safeguards shall review each application under section 103 or section 104 b. for a
construction permit or an operating license for a facility and shall submit a report thereon which
shall be made part of the record of the application and available to the public except to the
extent that security classification prevents disclosure.” The LMGS CP application was submitted
under section 103 of the AEA.
 H.K. Nieh                                     -2-



2. Important scope remains to be completed to support the operating license (OL) application
   including:

   a. Both fuel and structural materials are challenged by the peak temperatures predicted
      under limiting accident conditions. Consequently, fuel performance, mechanistic source
      term, functional containment, and graphite and metallic component performance require
      significant additional development.

   b. The applicant’s source‑term analysis employs a tristructural isotropic (TRISO) fuel
      diffusional‑release model derived from uranium dioxide (UO₂) correlations even though
      the Xe‑100 fuel form is uranium oxycarbide (UCO). Notably, data from the Department
      of Energy’s Advanced Gas Reactor (AGR) program show substantially lower cesium
      release from UCO. The OL application should present a fully consistent treatment of
      UCO TRISO fuel performance and the associated source term under normal and
      accident conditions, including uncertainties.

   c. Other safety topics warranting additional attention include the PRA of additional
      hazards (including external events and fire) and other operating states, passive reactor
      cavity cooling system (RCCS) performance, protection-system and
      nuclear-instrumentation diversity, fuel-handling and non-core source terms, and
      monitoring and inspectability.

BACKGROUND

On March 31, 2025, LME, a wholly owned subsidiary of The Dow Chemical Company,
submitted an application under Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50 to
construct LMGS adjacent to Dow's Seadrift Operations facility in Seadrift, Texas. The NRC
accepted the application for review on May 12, 2025. LMGS consists of four Xe-100 reactor
modules in a common nuclear island. Each reactor module consists of a reactor vessel
containing a 200 MWt (80 MWe), helium-cooled, graphite-moderated pebble-bed reactor (PBR)
using UCO TRISO particle fuel; a steam generator vessel housing a helical-tube steam
generator and two helium circulators; and a connecting cross vessel containing a hot gas duct.

LMGS is the first CP application for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) to use the
technology-inclusive, risk-informed, and performance-based licensing framework described in
Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.233, which endorses Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04, “Risk-
Informed Performance-Based Technology-Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light-Water Reactor
Licensing Basis Development,” often referred to as the Licensing Modernization Project (LMP).

The CP application identifies the required safety functions (RSF) as retention of radionuclides,
control of heat removal, control of heat generation, control of water and steam ingress, and
maintenance of geometry. The safety case is largely centered on ensuring retention of
radionuclides using a functional containment strategy. Key fission product barriers in the
functional containment approach include the UCO kernel, TRISO pyrocarbon and silicon
carbide (SiC) coatings, the fuel-free outer pebble graphitic layer, and the helium pressure
boundary (HPB). The thick concrete radiation shield structure around the reactor and the
reactor building are not credited as barriers. The remaining RSFs (control of heat removal,
control of heat generation, control of steam and air ingress, and maintenance of geometry) are
 H.K. Nieh                                     -3-



implemented using a mixture of redundant, diverse, passive, and inherent capabilities in the
design to ensure that challenges to the TRISO fuel are minimized and that the fuel and
structural materials remain inside their qualification envelopes.

The LMGS CP application builds upon several years of pre-application engagement and NRC
staff and ACRS review of TRs addressing the Xe-100 principal design criteria (PDC), fuel
qualification, transient and safety analysis methodology, mechanistic source term, and
qualification of the GOTHIC and Flownex analysis codes. Each of these approved TRs
established important elements of the analytical and regulatory framework used in the
application, subject to limitations and conditions.

DISCUSSION

The findings required for issuance of a CP are established in 10 CFR Part 50.35. Consistent
with RG 1.233, a PRA model provides the analytical foundation establishing design-specific
requirements and development activities. Model and design uncertainties are characterized
through sensitivity studies, bounding analyses, demonstrations of margin, and defined methods
and procedures. Our review focused on the unique, novel, and noteworthy topics affecting the
safety case, organized by RSF.2

RETENTION OF RADIONUCLIDES: Fuel performance, mechanistic source term, and
functional containment

Fuel performance, mechanistic source term, and functional containment warrant particular
attention in the development supporting the OL application because of their central roles in the
Xe-100 safety case. The fuel temperature exceeds both the historic TRISO UO2 fuel
qualification benchmark of 1600°C and the 1800°C value used in AGR UCO TRISO testing.3
Also, the expected peak burnup of the Xe-100 fuel is above the values achieved in the AGR
program for the Xe-100 TRISO particle design. Hence, additional fuel irradiation and high-
temperature testing is an essential part of the applicant’s fuel qualification program and
subsequent validation of the mechanistic source term.

We examined the applicability of the mechanistic source term models in the applicant’s
XSTERM computer code to UCO fuel. These models were derived in part from the German
UO2 TRISO experience. These UO2-based models predict significant SiC degradation at very
high temperature (> 1600°C) from carbon monoxide generated in UO2 during the fission
process. However, that degradation mechanism is absent in UCO. Accident-heating data from
TRISO UCO fuel shows very different behavior under postulated depressurized loss-of-force-
cooling (DLOFC) conditions, considered to be limiting. During AGR 300-hour heating tests at
1600°C, cesium release is approximately 300 times lower in UCO than in comparable TRISO
UO2 testing; at 1800°C, cesium release is approximately 10,000 times lower. Consequently,
the calculated doses in the CP application are likely conservative and not representative of

2 Consistent with Executive Order 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory

Commission,” dated May 23, 2025.
3 Accident heating tests from the AGR program demonstrated excellent performance for UCO

TRISO up to 1800°C. Results are documented in an Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)
UCO TRISO fuel performance TR accepted by the NRC in 2020.
 H.K. Nieh                                        -4-



expected UCO performance. We recommend the OL application present a fully consistent
treatment of UCO TRISO fuel performance and associated source term under normal and
accident conditions, including uncertainties.

Production fuel quality and the inherent variability of defect levels from fabrication are critical to
functional containment and the source-term basis. The OL source-term analysis should bound
fabrication defects, incremental particle failures, and radionuclide release measured in UCO
under conditions representative of Xe-100 service. These results may support lower releases
than estimated in the CP application, but that conclusion depends on qualification beyond AGR
service conditions and the integrated functional containment assessment.

The functional containment assessment must also establish the contribution of non-core
radionuclide inventories and associated credited barriers that limit radiological releases. The
CP application identifies radionuclide inventories contained in graphite dust, purification media,
fuel-handling system and spent fuel, and identifies the least-filtered release paths. Isolation and
confinement functions in the fuel handling system help limit non-core releases. Planned
component testing and dust characterization should strengthen the basis for valve and seal
reliability, pebble breakage, filter performance, isolation response, and the integrated non-core
source term.

We find the preliminary design, staff review, sensitivity analyses, and retention mechanisms
among multiple barriers provide an adequate CP-stage basis.

CONTROL OF HEAT REMOVAL: Passive and active heat removal

The applicant’s safety case identifies four core heat-removal modes under off-normal
conditions: heat transfer through the steam generators to the condenser when the steam
system is not isolated; the startup and shutdown system (SSS); active cooling via the
water-cooled RCCS; and safety-related passive RCCS cooling. The applicant’s PRA estimates
the loss of all four modes to be a very low-frequency event, with the passive RCCS operation
credited as the final line of defense.

For scenarios that rely on heat removal via the RCCS’s passive mode, the water inventory is
sized to maintain passive cooling for a minimum of 72 hours. During passive operation, heat
rejection to the environment through the RCCS may induce two-phase flow instabilities in the
standpipes, such as geysering, potentially impacting structural stability of the standpipes and
decay heat removal. LME plans to resolve this passive cooling challenge in the design prior to
submitting the OL application.

CONTROL OF HEAT GENERATION: Reactivity control and reactor protection systems

Online refueling provides operators a means for limiting excess core reactivity, while negative
fuel and moderator temperature feedback and two independent control rod systems provide
reactivity control and shutdown capability. Turning off the helium circulators reduces heat
removal and raises the core temperature; the resulting negative reactivity feedback will shut
down the reactor without any rod insertion. The negative reactivity satisfies the PDC 11
inherent-protection function. However, this may not maintain long-term subcriticality as the core
cools and xenon decays. In addition, the reactivity feedback may only take the reactor to a low
 H.K. Nieh                                      -5-



power state if there is not sufficient decay heat production in the fuel, such as when fresh fuel
is added to the pebble bed early in its approach to equilibrium. Nevertheless, inserting control
rods will shut down the reactor for all conditions.

The active shutdown functions depend upon the reactor protection system (RPS), reactivity
control and shutdown system (RCSS), and nuclear instrumentation system (NIS). The RCSS is
comprised of the reactivity control system (RCS) and the reserve shutdown system (RSS).
Both systems employ control rods to accomplish their safety function. Together with the
investment protection system (IPS) and distributed control system, these systems provide
normal reactivity control, automatic protective actuation, redundant gravity-driven rod insertion,
and maintenance of long-term subcriticality. Although the RPS and IPS provide diverse means
of initiating a reactor trip, both rely on data from the NIS, and the CP application does not
address diversity within that system. Final common-cause-failure analysis, including the role
and diversity of the NIS, remain for the OL application review.

The PDC 26 shutdown function is provided by two independent reactivity control systems (RCS
and RSS), each with nine rods. Each system can shut down the reactor, including scenarios
where one rod is assumed to be stuck out. Unlike light-water reactor general design criteria 26
in Appendix A of 10 CFR Part 50, Xe-100 PDC 26 does not require two shutdown systems
employing different design principles. The rod systems are independent but not diverse;
inherent negative temperature feedback (PDC 11) adds diversity to the overall reactivity-control
strategy. The NRC staff found this strategy acceptable for the CP stage. Although not credited,
defueling could provide an additional long-term defense-in-depth measure; the timing
associated with this shutdown capability should be quantified.

Overall, we find that the planned reactivity-control features provide a reasonable CP-stage
basis.

CONTROL OF STEAM AND AIR INGRESS: The role of isolation and break size

Failure of the HPB can expose fuel and graphite to steam or air, thereby degrading
radionuclide retention in fuel pebbles through oxidation of the graphite matrix and exposed fuel
kernels. These interactions may increase fission-product release and mobilize radionuclides
retained in graphite or deposited on primary-system surfaces and are accounted for in the
source term methodology.

The nuclear island feedwater isolation valves and nuclear island steam isolation valves
mitigate the consequences of a steam generator tube rupture by isolating the steam generator
from the feedwater and main steam systems to limit water and steam ingress into the primary
circuit. This depends on highly reliable steam generator isolation. In some steam generator
tube rupture events, operator action is credited to reinitiate cooling via the SSS through the
intact tube bundle after the ruptured bundle is identified. This is inconsistent with Section
6.4.12.2, “Steam Generator System Performance and Operation,” of the LMGS preliminary
safety analysis report, which states that the steam generator system performs its RSFs and
PRA safety functions without reliance on operator action. This inconsistency should be
reconciled in the OL application.
 H.K. Nieh                                      -6-



For air ingress, the amount of air entering the reactor is limited by the break size of pipes
attached to the HPB. Initial calculations show little oxidation of the graphite and fuel would
occur, mostly in the lower plenum region of the core. These calculations require validation for
the OL application. For both air and steam ingress, initial calculations show combustible gas
generation (CO, H2) remains below flammability levels. In addition, moisture and air ingress
testing is included in the LMGS research and development (R&D) plan to address fuel
behavior, fission-product transport, and source-term uncertainties.

MAINTENANCE OF GEOMETRY: Material qualification

Maintaining the geometry and structural integrity of Xe-100 structures, systems, and
components (SSCs) under operating and accident conditions is a required safety function. Key
considerations include irradiation and oxidation effects on graphite structures and
high-temperature creep, creep-fatigue, and strength limits for metallic supports, piping, and
internal components. Material qualification, including justification for service at conditions
beyond existing Code limits and supporting databases, is therefore a cross-cutting element of
the safety case.

The graphite structures must preserve core geometry, control-rod insertion, and passive
heat-transfer paths while accommodating irradiation effects, irradiation-induced creep,
cracking, wear, oxidation, and combined loads. Existing graphite-reactor experience provides a
substantial knowledge base that we judge to be generally consistent with the CP stage design
requirements. However, evaluations of supplier and grade-specific graphite properties
(especially at locations with high radiation dose), dimensional tolerances, inspection intervals,
and combined-load analyses remain for the OL application review.

The qualification envelope for several metallic materials must be expanded to encompass the
Xe-100 design temperatures. The CPA proposes 2¼% chromium (Cr) and 1% molybdenum
(Mo) in the control rod bellows and other applications of this alloy may be under consideration.
However, the creep, fatigue, and static-strength evaluations require extrapolation beyond the
approximately 300,000-hour American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and
Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code database for this material to support a 60-year life. Alloy 316H
(High-Carbon Austenitic Stainless Steel) is specified for the steam-system piping and valves
and is one of the candidate materials, along with Alloy 800H (a high-strength,
solution-annealed nickel-iron-chromium alloy), for steam-generator internal structures. Both
materials require extension of applicable ASME B&PV Code temperature and associated
creep-fatigue data. In addition, the Alloy 800H hot-gas duct may exceed the current 760°C
ASME B&PV Section III, Division 5 limit during Service Level B and higher conditions. Its low
allowable stress at these temperatures also makes differential-pressure loads important.
Detailed Division 5 thermal-mechanical evaluations for all operating and accident conditions,
justification of Code-data extensions, and treatment of extrapolation and model uncertainty for
each material selected for use at these elevated temperatures will be necessary for the OL
application review. The planned qualification and R&D programs provide a reasonable
completion path.

Monitoring is particularly important for the hot gas duct, defuel chute, graphite structures, and
core pedestal, where direct inspection for degradation is impractical. The preliminary design
identifies the conditions to be monitored, while planned sensor capability, placement,
 H.K. Nieh                                      -7-



qualification, surveillance, and acceptance criteria for establishing how degradation is detected
and addressed remain to be developed. We find these provisions provide a reasonable
CP-stage basis for monitoring component integrity as the design matures.

Risk-informed licensing basis, uncertainty, and cliff-edge effects

Consistent with RG 1.253, the CP-stage LMGS PRA addresses internal events at full power.
External hazards, other operating states, multi-module interactions, and common-cause
analyses remain for the OL application. Therefore, the OL application PRA should identify if an
external hazard could both initiate an event and disable credited SSCs, including those shared
among modules. The Committee observes that the iterative LMP process, as endorsed in RG
1.233, provides a pathway to address the additional PRA scope and manage uncertainties.

The assessment of cliff-edge effects extends PRA model completeness. The applicant’s initial
evaluations identified no cliff-edge effects, and the staff judged the CP-stage work sufficient.
Although TRISO fuel is resilient under severe time-at-temperature conditions, structural and
pressure-boundary systems preserving core geometry, core heat removal, and radionuclide
retention may reach their safety design limits first. A holistic search should therefore address
abrupt loss of these functions and associated radiological consequences. Integrated
quantification, uncertainty treatment, and confirmation of material and component margins
remain for the OL application.

The staff noted in its SER that the applicant’s evaluation of the balance between prevention
and mitigation—a PRA-centric approach supplemented by deterministic evaluations of
margin—does not address the balance holistically and is not consistent with how the balance
between prevention and mitigation has traditionally been assessed. We observe that the
applicant’s approach appears similar to that described in a 2009 Idaho National Laboratory
(INL) Next Generation Nuclear Plant Program white paper. In the white paper, the need to
define “mitigation” was framed in a different way for an HTGR. The traditional definition of
“mitigation,” which refers to limiting the consequences to the public after a significant fission
product release from fuel, does not directly apply to an HTGR because its accident sequences
do not result in release of a significant fraction of the fission product inventory from the TRISO
fuel. We encourage the applicant and staff to consider the insights from this white paper when
assessing the balance between prevention and mitigation in the OL application.

SUMMARY

The Xe-100 includes features that move away from the HTGR technology’s traditional passive
safety approach and associated design safety margins. This increases the importance of fuel
and materials qualifications and demonstrated defense-in-depth capability. Areas warranting
particular attention include:

•   Predicted peak accident temperatures above the historic 1600°C benchmark;

•   The UCO TRISO fuel service conditions beyond the AGR qualification basis;

•   High-dose irradiation effects on graphite reflectors, including evolving changes in
    mechanical properties, irradiation-induced creep, and dimensional stability;
 H.K. Nieh                                      -8-



•   High-temperature metallic-component performance over a 60-year design life, including
    creep, creep-fatigue, degradation, and extension of applicable ASME B&PV limitations with
    supporting data;

•   Passive RCCS that may experience two-phase flow instabilities in the standpipes
    potentially impacting structural stability of the standpipes and decay heat removal; and

•   Active isolation and actuation functions required to mitigate steam generator tube rupture.

Completion of the LME CP application Chapter 13 R&D program, the OL application PRA and
accident analyses, and other commitments will fully define safety margins. The OL application
should integrate these results with mechanistic source-term modeling and the functional
containment assessment.

Based on the matters considered in our review, we support issuance of the CP.

We are not requesting a formal response from the staff to this letter.

                                             Sincerely,



                                             Gregory H. Halnon
                                             Chairman
 H.K. Nieh                                   -9-
